expectedText:
PRIVATE NUISANCE BETWEEN NEIGHBORS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701

PURPOSE AND PARTIES: PRIVATE NUISANCE BETWEEN NEIGHBORS
Jordan Lee, who occupies or owns the real property located at 123 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party One"), and Morgan Casey, who occupies or owns the nearby or adjoining real property located at 125 Main St., Fresno, CA 93701 ("Party Two"), are parties to a dispute concerning property in Fresno County, California. The condition or activity this document concerns is described as follows: Outdoor machinery run nightly between 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. within 15 feet of the shared property line.

This document states facts about the part of California law that governs private nuisance — the body of law that addresses a use of one person's land that interferes with a neighbor's use and enjoyment of that neighbor's own land, as distinct from a physical trespass onto it. It draws on the Civil Code's nuisance provisions (Sections 3479, 3480, 3481, 3482, 3483, 3484, 3493, 3501, 3502, and 3503), on Code of Civil Procedure Sections 731 and 338, and on two published California Supreme Court decisions: San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, which describes the two elements a private nuisance claim requires beyond mere interference, and Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, which describes the difference between a "continuing" and a "permanent" nuisance and what that difference means for repeated lawsuits and for limitations periods.

This document states facts about that law. It does not tell Party One or Party Two what to do about the condition or activity described above, does not evaluate whether that condition or activity is or is not a nuisance under California law, and does not evaluate whether any claim or defense either party might raise would succeed.

HOW CALIFORNIA'S CIVIL CODE DEFINES A NUISANCE
California's Civil Code opens its nuisance provisions with a single definitional section that describes nuisance by listing categories of things rather than by naming elements of a lawsuit. As the statute is written, a thing can be a nuisance because it is injurious to health, because it is indecent or offensive to the senses, because it is an obstruction to the free use of property that interferes with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or because it unlawfully obstructs the free passage or use of certain waterways and public places. The clause about obstruction to the free use of property is the branch of the definition that neighbor-to-neighbor disputes most often involve. The Legislature amended this section in 1996 to add the illegal sale of controlled substances to the "injurious to health" category as a non-exclusive example.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Anything which is injurious to health, including, but not limited to, the illegal sale of controlled substances, or is indecent or offensive to the senses, or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property, or unlawfully obstructs the free passage or use, in the customary manner, of any navigable lake, or river, bay, stream, canal, or basin, or any public park, square, street, or highway, is a nuisance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3479, California Civil Code, general statutory definition of a nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3479.)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 3479 is a definition only. Its fetched text does not distinguish a public nuisance from a private one (adjoining sections quoted elsewhere in this document draw that line), does not state what a plaintiff must prove to recover damages or obtain an injunction, and does not define "offensive to the senses," "comfortable enjoyment of life or property," or any threshold of severity; California Supreme Court case law quoted elsewhere in this document supplies additional elements that the statutory text does not mention. The section's breadth has been described in case law as sweeping, but this clause does not characterize how broadly any court has applied it. The leginfo page for this section displays the amendment note "(Amended by Stats. 1996, Ch. 658, Sec. 1. Effective January 1, 1997.)"; this clause reports that note as displayed and does not independently verify the chaptered bill text.

PUBLIC NUISANCE, PRIVATE NUISANCE, AND A PRIVATE PERSON'S ACTION FOR A PUBLIC NUISANCE
The Civil Code sorts nuisances into two categories and defines only one of them affirmatively. A public nuisance is defined by the number of people it affects at the same time: it is one that affects an entire community or neighborhood, or any considerable number of persons, and the statute adds that the extent of annoyance or damage to particular individuals may be unequal without changing that classification. Private nuisance is then defined residually — every nuisance that does not fall within the public-nuisance definition is private. A separate section addresses the overlap between the two categories: it states that a private person may maintain an action for a public nuisance if the public nuisance is specially injurious to that person, but not otherwise.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A public nuisance is one which affects at the same time an entire community or neighborhood, or any considerable number of persons, although the extent of the annoyance or damage inflicted upon individuals may be unequal."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3480, California Civil Code, definition of a public nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3480.)
  "Every nuisance not included in the definition of the last section is private."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3481, California Civil Code, residual definition of a private nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3481.)
  "A private person may maintain an action for a public nuisance, if it is specially injurious to himself, but not otherwise."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3493, California Civil Code, private person's action for a public nuisance specially injurious to that person (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3493.)
  Known gap: The three quoted sections state classifications, not remedies or elements. They do not define "community," "neighborhood," "any considerable number of persons," or "specially injurious," and they do not state that the two categories are mutually exclusive in practice — the same condition may fall within both definitions, and Section 3493's existence presupposes that a public nuisance can also injure one person specially. Section 3493 retains the gender-specific pronoun "himself" from its 1872 enactment. On the leginfo page for Section 3480 the section number itself is displayed inside square brackets, as "[3480.]"; this clause reports that rendering without determining why the source displays it that way, and the bracketed number is not part of the quoted statutory text. That page also displays the note "(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 36. (AB 1170) Effective January 1, 2026.)"; the quoted text is the text the source displayed on the date stated in this clause, and this document did not independently verify the chaptered bill or compare the current text against the pre-2026 version.

THE TWO ELEMENTS A PRIVATE NUISANCE CLAIM REQUIRES BEYOND INTERFERENCE: FIRST, SUBSTANTIAL HARM
In San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court, the California Supreme Court described private nuisance as a nontrespassory interference with the private use and enjoyment of land, and contrasted it with trespass in two directions. On the one hand, nuisance liability does not require proof of damage to the plaintiff's property; interference with use and enjoyment can be enough. On the other hand, the court explained that private nuisance liability requires proof of two elements beyond the interference itself, a requirement the court traced to the reality that people living near one another unavoidably impose some annoyance on each other. The first of those two elements is that the invasion of the plaintiff's interest in the use and enjoyment of the land be substantial — that it caused substantial actual damage. The court described the measure of that element as objective rather than personal to the plaintiff, framed as the effect the invasion would have on persons of normal health and sensibilities living in the same community, and as a question of fact turning on each case's circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Plaintiffs attempt to state a cause of action for private nuisance, i.e., a nontrespassory interference with the private use and enjoyment of land."
  — San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, 937, California Supreme Court, describing private nuisance and its distinction from trespass (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607852/san-diego-gas-electric-co-v-superior-court/)
  "In further distinction to trespass, however, liability for private nuisance requires proof of two additional elements."
  — San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, 937, California Supreme Court, stating that private nuisance requires two elements beyond the interference itself (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607852/san-diego-gas-electric-co-v-superior-court/)
  "The degree of harm is to be judged by an objective standard, i.e., what effect would the invasion have on persons of normal health and sensibilities living in the same community?"
  — San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, 938, California Supreme Court, stating the objective standard for the substantial-harm element (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607852/san-diego-gas-electric-co-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court is a published California Supreme Court decision, but its discussion of these elements arose in a case about electric and magnetic fields from powerlines in which the court ultimately held the plaintiffs' claims were barred by the California Public Utilities Commission's exclusive jurisdiction; the elements discussion is the court's statement of the governing substantive law rather than the ground on which the case was resolved. The opinion expressly declined to decide whether a fear of future harm can support a private nuisance cause of action, noting a split between two Court of Appeal decisions on that question. The court's description of the "substantial actual damage" and objective-standard requirements is drawn from and cites secondary authorities (the Restatement Second of Torts, Prosser & Keeton, and Harper et al.); those secondary authorities were not independently fetched or verified in this research, and this clause relies only on the opinion's own fetched text. The opinion states no numeric threshold for what makes an invasion substantial. The case text was retrieved from CourtListener's opinion page for this decision, fetched twice — once through CourtListener's citation-lookup redirect for 13 Cal.4th 893 and once directly from the resulting opinion URL, with two different browser User-Agent strings — and the two extractions were byte-identical.

THE SECOND ELEMENT: THE INTERFERENCE MUST ALSO BE UNREASONABLE
The same California Supreme Court opinion describes the second additional element as superficially similar to the first but analytically distinct: an interference that is substantial must also be unreasonable. The court stated the primary test for unreasonableness as a weighing one — whether the gravity of the harm outweighs the social utility of the defendant's conduct, taking a number of factors into account. As with the substantiality element, the court described the standard as objective rather than turning on the particular plaintiff's own reaction, and described the question as one of fact for the trier of fact to resolve in light of all the circumstances of the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The primary test for determining whether the invasion is unreasonable is whether the gravity of the harm outweighs the social utility of the defendant’s conduct, taking a number of factors into account."
  — San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, 938, California Supreme Court, stating the primary test for whether an invasion is unreasonable (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607852/san-diego-gas-electric-co-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the California Supreme Court's statement of the unreasonableness test, which the opinion itself attributes to the Restatement Second of Torts and to Prosser & Keeton; those secondary sources were not independently fetched or verified here, and the court's own listing of "a number of factors" is a reference to Restatement sections 826 through 831 rather than an enumeration in the opinion's own text — so this clause does not state what those factors are. The opinion does not state how the weighing comes out in any particular category of neighbor dispute, and it resolved the case before it on preemption-style grounds (the Public Utilities Commission's exclusive jurisdiction) rather than by applying the weighing test to reach a merits result. The quoted sentence spans the opinion's star pagination between pages 938 and 939; the page number given in the citation is the page on which the quoted sentence begins.

THE REMEDIES THE STATUTES NAME FOR A PRIVATE NUISANCE
The Civil Code names two remedies against a private nuisance: a civil action, or abatement. The Code of Civil Procedure then describes who may bring the civil action and what a judgment in it can do. Under that section, an action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened, by a nuisance as the Civil Code defines it, and the judgment in that action may enjoin or abate the nuisance as well as award damages for it. The same section separately authorizes a district attorney, county counsel, or city attorney to bring an action in the name of the people of the State of California to abate a public nuisance, and directs those officers to bring such an action whenever directed by the county board of supervisors or by a city's or town's legislative authority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The remedies against a private nuisance are:
1. A civil action; or,
2. Abatement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3501, California Civil Code, remedies against a private nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3501.)
  "An action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened by a nuisance, as defined in Section 3479 of the Civil Code, and by the judgment in that action the nuisance may be enjoined or abated as well as damages recovered therefor."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 731, California Code of Civil Procedure, who may bring a nuisance action and what the judgment may do (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=731.)
  Known gap: Code of Civil Procedure Section 731 states who may sue and what relief a judgment may grant; it does not state a limitations period, does not state what must be proved, and does not state when a court will grant an injunction rather than damages. In the fetched leginfo page the sentence referring to the public-nuisance definition contains a mid-sentence line break in the source between "Section 3480" and "of the Civil Code"; that benign line-wrap artifact has been normalized to a single space in the quotation reproduced here, with no other change to the text. Civil Code Section 3501's text is rendered by the source as three separate paragraph elements (the introductory line and the two numbered remedies), with a non-breaking space after each numeral; the quotation here reproduces those three parts as three lines and normalizes each non-breaking space to an ordinary space, with no other change to the text.

ABATEMENT BY THE INJURED PERSON, AND THE LIMITS THE STATUTES PLACE ON IT
Alongside a civil action, the Civil Code recognizes abatement by the injured person as a remedy against a private nuisance, and it states limits on that remedy in the same breath as it grants it. The statute says a person injured by a private nuisance may abate it by removing — or, if necessary, destroying — the thing that constitutes the nuisance, but conditions that on doing so without committing a breach of the peace and without doing unnecessary injury. A companion section adds a notice condition for one particular situation: where the private nuisance results from a mere omission of the wrongdoer and cannot be abated without entering on the wrongdoer's land, reasonable notice must be given to the wrongdoer before entering to abate it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A person injured by a private nuisance may abate it by removing, or, if necessary, destroying the thing which constitutes the nuisance, without committing a breach of the peace, or doing unnecessary injury."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3502, California Civil Code, abatement of a private nuisance by the injured person (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3502.)
  "Where a private nuisance results from a mere omission of the wrongdoer, and cannot be abated without entering upon his land, reasonable notice must be given to him before entering to abate it."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3503, California Civil Code, notice required before entering another's land to abate a nuisance arising from an omission (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3503.)
  Known gap: These two sections, enacted in 1872 and never amended, state the abatement remedy in general terms and leave the operative limits undefined: their text does not define "breach of the peace," does not define "unnecessary injury," does not say how much notice is "reasonable" or in what form it must be given, and does not distinguish a "mere omission" from affirmative conduct. Section 3503 retains the gender-specific pronouns "his" and "him" from its original enactment. Neither section states what happens if a person who abates exceeds these limits, and neither section addresses how self-help abatement interacts with other bodies of law that may independently govern the same conduct. This document quotes only the statutory text; it does not summarize case law construing these two sections, and it does not evaluate whether any particular act of removal or destruction would fall within them.

A LATER OWNER WHO DOES NOT ABATE A CONTINUING NUISANCE CREATED BY AN EARLIER OWNER
One Civil Code section addresses what happens when property changes hands while a nuisance on it continues. It states that every successive owner of property who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance on the property, or in the use of the property, that was created by a former owner is liable for it in the same manner as the person who first created it. The rule as written turns on neglecting to abate a nuisance that is continuing, rather than on the later owner having created or participated in creating the condition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Every successive owner of property who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance upon, or in the use of, such property, created by a former owner, is liable therefor in the same manner as the one who first created it."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3483, California Civil Code, liability of a successive owner who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3483.)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 3483 has not been amended since its 1872 enactment. Its text does not define "continuing nuisance" — a distinction California Supreme Court case law develops and that another clause of this document addresses — does not state how long a successive owner has before neglect is established, does not state whether the successive owner must have known of the condition, and does not address whether the former owner who created the nuisance remains liable as well. This clause states what the statute says; it does not evaluate whether any particular condition is continuing, whether any particular owner has neglected to abate one, or how this section interacts with agreements between a seller and a buyer.

ABATING A NUISANCE DOES NOT EXTINGUISH A CLAIM FOR DAMAGES ALREADY CAUSED
A short Civil Code section addresses the relationship between stopping a nuisance and recovering for the harm it has already caused. It states that the abatement of a nuisance does not prejudice the right of any person to recover damages for the nuisance's past existence. On the statute's own terms, the fact that a condition has been removed, corrected, or stopped — whether voluntarily, by agreement, or by court order — does not by itself eliminate a claim for damages attributable to the period when the condition existed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "The abatement of a nuisance does not prejudice the right of any person to recover damages for its past existence."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3484, California Civil Code, abatement does not prejudice the right to damages for past existence of the nuisance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3484.)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 3484, enacted in 1872 and never amended, is a single sentence. Its text does not state who must have performed the abatement for the rule to apply, does not state any limitations period for the damages claim it preserves (limitations questions are addressed by other provisions and by case law, including the material in this document's clause on continuing and permanent nuisances), and does not state what damages are recoverable or how they are measured. It does not address the separate question of whether a private settlement or release between the parties might independently bar a damages claim. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular condition has in fact been abated.

THE STATUTORY-AUTHORITY LIMIT ON WHAT CAN BE DEEMED A NUISANCE
The Civil Code's general nuisance principles include a section that removes certain conduct from the category of nuisance altogether. It states that nothing which is done or maintained under the express authority of a statute can be deemed a nuisance. The provision is framed as a categorical statement about what can be deemed a nuisance, rather than as a defense that a court weighs against the harm caused, and it is keyed to express statutory authority for the thing done or maintained.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Nothing which is done or maintained under the express authority of a statute can be deemed a nuisance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3482, California Civil Code, conduct done or maintained under the express authority of a statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3482.)
  Known gap: Civil Code Section 3482, enacted in 1872 and never amended, is one sentence and defines none of its own operative terms: it does not say what makes authority "express" as opposed to implied or general, does not say whether a permit, license, ordinance, or regulation counts as a "statute" for this purpose, and does not address conduct that exceeds whatever authority a statute confers. California case law has construed the section's reach, including how narrowly "express authority" is read; no such case was fetched or verified in this research, so this clause states only the statutory text and does not report how any court has applied it. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular activity is authorized by statute.

CONTINUING NUISANCE VERSUS PERMANENT NUISANCE, AND WHY THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS
In Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority, the California Supreme Court described two classifications that have emerged in nuisance law and that determine both the remedies available and the applicable limitations period. A permanent nuisance is one where, by one act, a permanent injury is done and damages are assessed once for all; the court noted that cases treating a nuisance as unquestionably permanent have involved solid structures, and that in such cases plaintiffs ordinarily must bring one action for all past, present, and future damage within three years after the permanent nuisance is erected. A continuing nuisance, by contrast, is a use that may be discontinued at any time; persons harmed by it may bring successive actions for damages until the nuisance is abated, with recovery in each action limited to injury actually suffered before that action was commenced and with prospective damages unavailable. The court described an ongoing or repeated disturbance caused by noise, vibration, or foul odor as the classic example of a continuing nuisance. The three-year period the court referred to corresponds to the Code of Civil Procedure's limitations section for an action for trespass upon or injury to real property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "In such cases, plaintiffs ordinarily are required to bring one action for all past, present and future damage within three years after the permanent nuisance is erected."
  — Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869, California Supreme Court, on the one-action rule and three-year period for a permanent nuisance (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1115893/baker-v-burbank-glendale-pasadena-airport-authority/)
  "On the other hand, if a nuisance is a use which may be discontinued at any time, it is considered continuing in character and persons harmed by it may bring successive actions for damages until the nuisance is abated."
  — Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869, California Supreme Court, defining a continuing nuisance and the right to bring successive actions (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1115893/baker-v-burbank-glendale-pasadena-airport-authority/)
  "Recovery is limited, however, to actual injury suffered prior to commencement of each action. Prospective damages are unavailable."
  — Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869, California Supreme Court, limiting recovery in each successive action to injury already suffered (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1115893/baker-v-burbank-glendale-pasadena-airport-authority/)
  "The classic example of a continuing nuisance is an ongoing or repeated disturbance, such as the one before us today, caused by noise, vibration or foul odor."
  — Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869-870, California Supreme Court, naming the classic example of a continuing nuisance (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1115893/baker-v-burbank-glendale-pasadena-airport-authority/)
  "An action for trespass upon or injury to real property."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 338(b), California Code of Civil Procedure, three-year limitations period for trespass upon or injury to real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=338.)
  Known gap: Baker is a published California Supreme Court decision, decided by a divided court — the fetched text includes a dissent — and the quotations used here are taken from the majority opinion. Baker arose from aircraft noise, smoke, and vibration from a public airport and involved a public entity, so parts of its reasoning address matters not present in a dispute between private neighbors, including a shorter claim-presentation period for claims against public entities under Government Code Section 911.2 and federal constraints on enjoining flight operations. Baker's holding is that the plaintiffs could elect to treat the airport nuisance as continuing and that the limitations period therefore did not bar their claims; the opinion does not supply a general test that resolves how any particular neighbor-to-neighbor condition should be classified. Code of Civil Procedure Section 338 is quoted here only for its opening words and its subdivision (b); this document does not analyze which limitations statute applies to any particular nuisance claim, and Baker itself refers to more than one limitations provision. The case text was retrieved from CourtListener's opinion page for this decision, fetched twice — once through CourtListener's citation-lookup redirect for 39 Cal.3d 862 and once directly from the resulting opinion URL, with two different browser User-Agent strings — and the two extractions were byte-identical.

expectedJSON.body: In San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court, the California Supreme Court described private nuisance as a nontrespassory interference with the private use and enjoyment of land, and contrasted it with trespass in two directions. On the one hand, nuisance liability does not require proof of damage to the plaintiff's property; interference with use and enjoyment can be enough. On the other hand, the court explained that private nuisance liability requires proof of two elements beyond the interference itself, a requirement the court traced to the reality that people living near one another unavoidably impose some annoyance on each other. The first of those two elements is that the invasion of the plaintiff's interest in the use and enjoyment of the land be substantial — that it caused substantial actual damage. The court described the measure of that element as objective rather than personal to the plaintiff, framed as the effect the invasion would have on persons of normal health and sensibilities living in the same community, and as a question of fact turning on each case's circumstances.

citations.cite: California Supreme Court, describing private nuisance and its distinction from trespass
citations.quote: Plaintiffs attempt to state a cause of action for private nuisance, i.e., a nontrespassory interference with the private use and enjoyment of land.

citations.quote: In further distinction to trespass, however, liability for private nuisance requires proof of two additional elements.

citations.case: San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court (1996) 13 Cal.4th 893, 938
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, stating the objective standard for the substantial-harm element
citations.quote: The degree of harm is to be judged by an objective standard, i.e., what effect would the invasion have on persons of normal health and sensibilities living in the same community?

expectedJSON.gap: San Diego Gas & Electric Co. v. Superior Court is a published California Supreme Court decision, but its discussion of these elements arose in a case about electric and magnetic fields from powerlines in which the court ultimately held the plaintiffs' claims were barred by the California Public Utilities Commission's exclusive jurisdiction; the elements discussion is the court's statement of the governing substantive law rather than the ground on which the case was resolved. The opinion expressly declined to decide whether a fear of future harm can support a private nuisance cause of action, noting a split between two Court of Appeal decisions on that question. The court's description of the "substantial actual damage" and objective-standard requirements is drawn from and cites secondary authorities (the Restatement Second of Torts, Prosser & Keeton, and Harper et al.); those secondary authorities were not independently fetched or verified in this research, and this clause relies only on the opinion's own fetched text. The opinion states no numeric threshold for what makes an invasion substantial. The case text was retrieved from CourtListener's opinion page for this decision, fetched twice — once through CourtListener's citation-lookup redirect for 13 Cal.4th 893 and once directly from the resulting opinion URL, with two different browser User-Agent strings — and the two extractions were byte-identical.

expectedJSON.body: The same California Supreme Court opinion describes the second additional element as superficially similar to the first but analytically distinct: an interference that is substantial must also be unreasonable. The court stated the primary test for unreasonableness as a weighing one — whether the gravity of the harm outweighs the social utility of the defendant's conduct, taking a number of factors into account. As with the substantiality element, the court described the standard as objective rather than turning on the particular plaintiff's own reaction, and described the question as one of fact for the trier of fact to resolve in light of all the circumstances of the case.

citations.quote: The primary test for determining whether the invasion is unreasonable is whether the gravity of the harm outweighs the social utility of the defendant’s conduct, taking a number of factors into account.

The opinion does not state how the weighing comes out in any particular category of neighbor dispute, and it resolved the case before it on preemption-style grounds (the Public Utilities Commission's exclusive jurisdiction) rather than by applying the weighing test to reach a merits result. The quoted sentence spans the opinion's star pagination between pages 938 and 939; the page number given in the citation is the page on which the quoted sentence begins.

expectedJSON.body: The Civil Code names two remedies against a private nuisance: a civil action, or abatement. The Code of Civil Procedure then describes who may bring the civil action and what a judgment in it can do. Under that section, an action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened, by a nuisance as the Civil Code defines it, and the judgment in that action may enjoin or abate the nuisance as well as award damages for it. The same section separately authorizes a district attorney, county counsel, or city attorney to bring an action in the name of the people of the State of California to abate a public nuisance, and directs those officers to bring such an action whenever directed by the county board of supervisors or by a city's or town's legislative authority.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, remedies against a private nuisance
citations.quote:
The remedies against a private nuisance are:
1. A civil action; or,
2. Abatement.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, who may bring a nuisance action and what the judgment may do
citations.quote: An action may be brought by any person whose property is injuriously affected, or whose personal enjoyment is lessened by a nuisance, as defined in Section 3479 of the Civil Code, and by the judgment in that action the nuisance may be enjoined or abated as well as damages recovered therefor.

expectedJSON.gap: Code of Civil Procedure Section 731 states who may sue and what relief a judgment may grant; it does not state a limitations period, does not state what must be proved, and does not state when a court will grant an injunction rather than damages. In the fetched leginfo page the sentence referring to the public-nuisance definition contains a mid-sentence line break in the source between "Section 3480" and "of the Civil Code"; that benign line-wrap artifact has been normalized to a single space in the quotation reproduced here, with no other change to the text. Civil Code Section 3501's text is rendered by the source as three separate paragraph elements (the introductory line and the two numbered remedies), with a non-breaking space after each numeral; the quotation here reproduces those three parts as three lines and normalizes each non-breaking space to an ordinary space, with no other change to the text.

expectedJSON.body: Alongside a civil action, the Civil Code recognizes abatement by the injured person as a remedy against a private nuisance, and it states limits on that remedy in the same breath as it grants it. The statute says a person injured by a private nuisance may abate it by removing — or, if necessary, destroying — the thing that constitutes the nuisance, but conditions that on doing so without committing a breach of the peace and without doing unnecessary injury. A companion section adds a notice condition for one particular situation: where the private nuisance results from a mere omission of the wrongdoer and cannot be abated without entering on the wrongdoer's land, reasonable notice must be given to the wrongdoer before entering to abate it.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, abatement of a private nuisance by the injured person
citations.quote: A person injured by a private nuisance may abate it by removing, or, if necessary, destroying the thing which constitutes the nuisance, without committing a breach of the peace, or doing unnecessary injury.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, notice required before entering another's land to abate a nuisance arising from an omission
citations.quote: Where a private nuisance results from a mere omission of the wrongdoer, and cannot be abated without entering upon his land, reasonable notice must be given to him before entering to abate it.

expectedJSON.gap: These two sections, enacted in 1872 and never amended, state the abatement remedy in general terms and leave the operative limits undefined: their text does not define "breach of the peace," does not define "unnecessary injury," does not say how much notice is "reasonable" or in what form it must be given, and does not distinguish a "mere omission" from affirmative conduct. Section 3503 retains the gender-specific pronouns "his" and "him" from its original enactment. Neither section states what happens if a person who abates exceeds these limits, and neither section addresses how self-help abatement interacts with other bodies of law that may independently govern the same conduct. This document quotes only the statutory text; it does not summarize case law construing these two sections, and it does not evaluate whether any particular act of removal or destruction would fall within them.

expectedJSON.body: One Civil Code section addresses what happens when property changes hands while a nuisance on it continues. It states that every successive owner of property who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance on the property, or in the use of the property, that was created by a former owner is liable for it in the same manner as the person who first created it. The rule as written turns on neglecting to abate a nuisance that is continuing, rather than on the later owner having created or participated in creating the condition.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, liability of a successive owner who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance
citations.quote: Every successive owner of property who neglects to abate a continuing nuisance upon, or in the use of, such property, created by a former owner, is liable therefor in the same manner as the one who first created it.

expectedJSON.gap: Civil Code Section 3483 has not been amended since its 1872 enactment. Its text does not define "continuing nuisance" — a distinction California Supreme Court case law develops and that another clause of this document addresses — does not state how long a successive owner has before neglect is established, does not state whether the successive owner must have known of the condition, and does not address whether the former owner who created the nuisance remains liable as well. This clause states what the statute says; it does not evaluate whether any particular condition is continuing, whether any particular owner has neglected to abate one, or how this section interacts with agreements between a seller and a buyer.

expectedJSON.body: A short Civil Code section addresses the relationship between stopping a nuisance and recovering for the harm it has already caused. It states that the abatement of a nuisance does not prejudice the right of any person to recover damages for the nuisance's past existence. On the statute's own terms, the fact that a condition has been removed, corrected, or stopped — whether voluntarily, by agreement, or by court order — does not by itself eliminate a claim for damages attributable to the period when the condition existed.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, abatement does not prejudice the right to damages for past existence of the nuisance
citations.quote: The abatement of a nuisance does not prejudice the right of any person to recover damages for its past existence.

expectedJSON.gap: Civil Code Section 3484, enacted in 1872 and never amended, is a single sentence. Its text does not state who must have performed the abatement for the rule to apply, does not state any limitations period for the damages claim it preserves (limitations questions are addressed by other provisions and by case law, including the material in this document's clause on continuing and permanent nuisances), and does not state what damages are recoverable or how they are measured. It does not address the separate question of whether a private settlement or release between the parties might independently bar a damages claim. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular condition has in fact been abated.

expectedJSON.body: The Civil Code's general nuisance principles include a section that removes certain conduct from the category of nuisance altogether. It states that nothing which is done or maintained under the express authority of a statute can be deemed a nuisance. The provision is framed as a categorical statement about what can be deemed a nuisance, rather than as a defense that a court weighs against the harm caused, and it is keyed to express statutory authority for the thing done or maintained.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, conduct done or maintained under the express authority of a statute
citations.quote: Nothing which is done or maintained under the express authority of a statute can be deemed a nuisance.

expectedJSON.gap: Civil Code Section 3482, enacted in 1872 and never amended, is one sentence and defines none of its own operative terms: it does not say what makes authority "express" as opposed to implied or general, does not say whether a permit, license, ordinance, or regulation counts as a "statute" for this purpose, and does not address conduct that exceeds whatever authority a statute confers. California case law has construed the section's reach, including how narrowly "express authority" is read; no such case was fetched or verified in this research, so this clause states only the statutory text and does not report how any court has applied it. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular activity is authorized by statute.

expectedJSON.body: In Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority, the California Supreme Court described two classifications that have emerged in nuisance law and that determine both the remedies available and the applicable limitations period. A permanent nuisance is one where, by one act, a permanent injury is done and damages are assessed once for all; the court noted that cases treating a nuisance as unquestionably permanent have involved solid structures, and that in such cases plaintiffs ordinarily must bring one action for all past, present, and future damage within three years after the permanent nuisance is erected. A continuing nuisance, by contrast, is a use that may be discontinued at any time; persons harmed by it may bring successive actions for damages until the nuisance is abated, with recovery in each action limited to injury actually suffered before that action was commenced and with prospective damages unavailable. The court described an ongoing or repeated disturbance caused by noise, vibration, or foul odor as the classic example of a continuing nuisance. The three-year period the court referred to corresponds to the Code of Civil Procedure's limitations section for an action for trespass upon or injury to real property.

citations.case: Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, on the one-action rule and three-year period for a permanent nuisance
citations.quote: In such cases, plaintiffs ordinarily are required to bring one action for all past, present and future damage within three years after the permanent nuisance is erected.

citations.case: Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, defining a continuing nuisance and the right to bring successive actions
citations.quote: On the other hand, if a nuisance is a use which may be discontinued at any time, it is considered continuing in character and persons harmed by it may bring successive actions for damages until the nuisance is abated.

citations.case: Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, limiting recovery in each successive action to injury already suffered
citations.quote: Recovery is limited, however, to actual injury suffered prior to commencement of each action. Prospective damages are unavailable.

citations.case: Baker v. Burbank-Glendale-Pasadena Airport Authority (1985) 39 Cal.3d 862, 869-870
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, naming the classic example of a continuing nuisance
citations.quote: The classic example of a continuing nuisance is an ongoing or repeated disturbance, such as the one before us today, caused by noise, vibration or foul odor.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, three-year limitations period for trespass upon or injury to real property
citations.quote: An action for trespass upon or injury to real property.

expectedJSON.gap: Baker is a published California Supreme Court decision, decided by a divided court — the fetched text includes a dissent — and the quotations used here are taken from the majority opinion. Baker arose from aircraft noise, smoke, and vibration from a public airport and involved a public entity, so parts of its reasoning address matters not present in a dispute between private neighbors, including a shorter claim-presentation period for claims against public entities under Government Code Section 911.2 and federal constraints on enjoining flight operations. Baker's holding is that the plaintiffs could elect to treat the airport nuisance as continuing and that the limitations period therefore did not bar their claims; the opinion does not supply a general test that resolves how any particular neighbor-to-neighbor condition should be classified. Code of Civil Procedure Section 338 is quoted here only for its opening words and its subdivision (b); this document does not analyze which limitations statute applies to any particular nuisance claim, and Baker itself refers to more than one limitations provision.
